unit.name: Issues and Impact
unit.subtitle: Environmental impact, ethical and legal issues, AI accountability, intellectual property and cybersecurity

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write that a syntax error is 'a spelling mistake' or 'a grammar mistake' in isolation. Examiners reject this as ambiguous because it could equally describe a logic error. The correct definition is that a syntax error means the rules of the programming language have been broken.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com (accessed 2026)

common_misconceptions.misconception: When asked the output of a relational expression such as a > b, students give 'yes/no' rather than 'True/False'. Examiners require the Boolean output type.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students correctly write height × width × colour depth but omit the unit 'pixels' for height and width. The unit is required for marks. Some students also include colour depth when only width × height is asked for, and vice versa.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse tebibytes (1024^4 bytes, binary) with terabytes (10^12 bytes, decimal) and miss the kibi/mebi/gibi/tebi progression. Many cannot correctly state how many bytes are in a tebibyte. Edexcel uses BINARY multiples (1024-based).
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1 + specification 2.3.1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: When asked to name a network protocol, some students give a file format such as .mp3 or .jpg. Protocols are rules for communication (HTTP, TCP, IMAP), not file types.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.topic: TCP/IP link layer vs network layer
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse the link layer (which deals with MAC addresses and the physical network medium) with the internet/network layer (which deals with IP addresses and routing). Few candidates can describe MAC addresses' role at the link layer.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2024, Paper 1, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students comment every line of Python, sometimes producing more comment lines than code lines. Examiners want comments to explain the LOGIC, placed at the start of blocks of code — not per-line restatements of what the code obviously does.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Examiner Report June 2022, Paper 2, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students try to use AQA-style or OCR-style pseudocode (FOR..ENDFOR, ←). Edexcel's spec footnote is clear that pseudocode is 'an informal written description of a program' with NO strict syntax requirement — plain English is acceptable.
common_misconceptions.source: Edexcel 1CP2 Specification, footnote to topic 1.2, qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students compress the three-stage cycle into 'fetch and execute' and omit the decode stage. The spec explicitly states three stages in 3.1.1.
Students use the terms function and procedure interchangeably. Edexcel 6.6.2 is precise: a function MUST return a value, a procedure must NOT return a value. Both may or may not take parameters.

student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Define: Vague or ambiguous definitions that could apply to multiple terms — for example, defining a syntax error as 'a mistake' which equally describes a logic or runtime error. Use the exact spec phrasing where possible.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain: Students give a description (statement of fact) instead of an explanation (statement of fact + reasoning or consequence). Examiner mark scheme requires each marking point to be linked to a justification.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Complete a Trace Table: Students add extra rows for iterations that didn't happen, or skip the update of a counter variable across rows. Drill the discipline of one row per state change.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Discuss: Students list arguments on one side only. The Discuss command word requires identifying the issue, exploring ALL aspects, and investigating by reasoning. Use a two-sided structure with evaluation.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Complete an Algorithm: Students lose marks for incomplete control flow, missing loop termination, or wrong output. Practise scaffolding: identify inputs, define the process step-by-step, define the output, then write.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Write a Subprogram: Common errors: function does not return a value when required; parameters are not used inside the body; identifier names don't match those in the calling code. Practise signature-first, body-second, return-third.

topic_weighting_notes: Paper 1 (50%, 75 marks, 1h 30m) covers topics 1–5 with one question per topic. Topic balance is roughly equal across the five questions but topic 1 (computational thinking) and topic 6 (programming) carry the cognitive load of the whole qualification.
Paper 2 (50%, 75 marks, 2h, onscreen Python) is six compulsory questions all drawn from topic 6. Half the course's lesson time should sit on programming.
Examiner reports consistently flag the data-representation calculations (tebibytes, image file sizes) as low-scoring — allocate strong worked examples here.
The four-layer TCP/IP model and protocol mapping are examined every year as 4–6 marks — drill the layer-to-protocol matching.
Cybersecurity (5.3) is split into threats (5.3.1) and protections (5.3.2) — both appear in every Paper 1 series, typically 4–6 marks.

Paper 2 Amend questions (5–15 marks) require students to read existing code and modify it. Paper 2 Write questions (5–15 marks) require fresh code. Both command words appear every series — practise both.
current_spec_changes: The Programming Language Subset (PLS) is updated annually. Version 6 (Summer 2025) clarified the two supported list dimensions and amended string.format and built-in subprogram descriptions. The latest PLS version is the authoritative reference for what Python features are examinable.
Python 3 is the only assessed language for Paper 2. The specification mentions that any version of a Python 3 interpreter is acceptable.
Specification first teaching was September 2020, first certification 2022. No major spec rewrites since. The Programming Language Subset is the only document that updates annually.
pedagogical_notes: EEF cognitive science evidence review (2021) supports worked examples as the highest-impact strategy for new programming content. Each programming lesson should walk through a fully-coded example before the practice section asks students to write their own.

PRIMM (Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, Make) is the most-cited pedagogy for GCSE programming. Particularly effective for Paper 2 Amend questions, where students must read existing code before modifying it. Use predict-then-trace as a routine for new code snippets.

EEF guidance on retrieval practice (2024 blog series) recommends spaced, conceptual retrieval rather than recognition. Knowledge checks should use fill-in-the-blank and short-answer formats for key vocabulary (Boolean, syntax error, kibibyte) rather than multiple choice for definitions.

EEF FAME framework for worked examples (alternation, fading, modelling, examining) maps directly onto programming pedagogy: alternate worked examples with similar problems, fade scaffolding as students gain confidence.
Dual coding pairs well with trace tables, flowcharts and TCP/IP layer diagrams. Use a visual paired with prose for any algorithm or networking concept.

Edexcel's spec is deliberately informal about pseudocode (an explicit footnote in 1.2). Content should mirror this — show plain-English step-by-step descriptions, not a formal pseudocode dialect, so students don't lose marks by misremembering syntax they were never required to learn.

lessons_in_batch.title: Environmental, Ethical and Legal Issues
lessons_in_batch.description: The energy cost of digital devices, e-waste, privacy and data protection, and intellectual property law.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L1 (Ethical and Legal Issues) overlaps on privacy and IP but bundles autonomous vehicles. Edexcel separates these — autonomous vehicles is in 5.2.2 (next lesson). Environmental section (5.1.1) is brief in Edexcel — energy, manufacture, replacement cycle, disposal — combine with ethical/legal here for a strong unit lesson. Edexcel splits IP into four categories (copyright, patents, trademarks, licencing) and examines each as distinct. Add brief explainers of each. Drop AQA's autonomous-vehicles content and mobile/wearable tech.

lessons_in_batch.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Robotics
lessons_in_batch.description: Accountability, safety, algorithmic bias and legal liability for AI and autonomous systems.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L2 (Autonomous Vehicles and Environmental Impacts) covers self-driving cars. Edexcel 5.2.2 is broader: AI, machine learning AND robotics, with four named ethical issues (accountability, safety, algorithmic bias, legal liability). Build the lesson around those four issues with a worked example for each (e.g. algorithmic bias = COMPAS recidivism case framed generically without naming specific datasets). Self-driving cars become ONE example of robotics here, not the whole lesson. Discuss (6-mark) practice question fits this topic perfectly per Edexcel's command-word taxonomy.

lessons_in_batch.title: Cybersecurity: Threats and Protection
lessons_in_batch.description: How malware, social engineering and exploits attack digital systems, and the layered defences that protect them.

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA L3 (Cyber Security Threats) covers malware and social engineering. ~65% transferable. Edexcel 5.3.1 has a WIDER malware list — adds worms, ransomware, key loggers (AQA tightly limits to virus/trojan/spyware). Use Edexcel's full list. Edexcel 5.3.2 names exactly five protections (anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup, recovery) — restructure as the five protections. Drop AQA-specific terms like 'blagging', 'shouldering' (Edexcel keeps social engineering at a higher level). Add a worked example of a layered defence strategy combining all five.
